rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding portrait of Quraysh leadership as liars and backbiters leads to the point that its violators of God's bounds also usurp human rights.
rows.anchor: the whole edifice of their leadership stood on lies, back-biting and humiliating others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although ‘forbidders of good’ generally obstruct virtue, here the phrase especially depicts misers who neither give to the poor nor tolerate others giving, and try to make others miserly to conceal their own meanness.
rows.anchor: they want that others too, should become misers like themselves so that they are able to hide their own miserliness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired terms distinguish usurping others’ rights from failing to fulfill rights owed to them: ʿatad names the first sin and ithm the second.
rows.anchor: first type of sin and the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Cruel and ruthless’ describes the inner aspect of the preceding traits; a miser is necessarily cruel, as illustrated by the Qur’an’s description of the one who drives away an orphan.
rows.anchor: A person who is stingy, shall necessarily be cruel. This is only the inner aspect of the traits mentioned earlier

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lexicographers explain zanīm as an outsider attaching himself to a clan that does not need him; the word derives from a goat’s dangling neck gland, and narratives give Akhnas and al-Walīd as claimed-lineage examples.
rows.anchor: a person who associates himself with the lineage of a clan whereas he actually does not belong to it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People who falsely attach themselves to superior lineages are show-offs, given to flattery and false displays of clan pride to gain credibility.
rows.anchor: Such people have a habit of flattery and sycophancy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such rootless Qurayshites led opposition to the Prophet, invoking Quraysh unity; parasites claiming greater loyalty became custodians of jāhiliyyah traditions, a trait fueled by inferiority and low confidence.
rows.anchor: there are some parasites who claim to be more loyal than the real members of the clan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children should have led these people to gratitude, obedience, and support for truth; instead they became ungrateful and defiant, failing God’s test of blessings.
rows.anchor: the purpose of God in blessing people with favours is to test them, whether they become grateful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their arrogance makes them dismiss accounts of destroyed nations as ancient stories unrelated to the present, rejecting both the prophetic narrator and the warnings’ force.
rows.anchor: they make fun of them when their accounts are mentioned to them. They regard them to be ancient stories

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘trunk’ is a metaphor for the noses they hold high: denying obvious truth to preserve pride makes the nose an inflated trunk that God will brand in public humiliation.
rows.anchor: Here it is used as a metaphor for the noses of such people because they were opposing the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard parable exposes the hollowness of Quraysh leaders’ authority: God can remove it instantly, after which their grief and repentance will be useless.
rows.anchor: their authority which has made them so conceited and proud that they are making fun of the warnings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural pronoun ‘them’ refers to the previously described people collectively, confirming that the portrait is of Quraysh leadership as a whole rather than one individual.
rows.anchor: this character is not that of a specific individual; it is that of the total leadership of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in ‘the orchard’ is generic in parables, painting a complete situation rather than identifying a particular orchard or historical owners in Yemen or Sana.
rows.anchor: Their purpose is only to portray the overall situation so that the reader gets to know the complete picture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owners confidently swore they would harvest the next morning because they believed their orchard had survived every weather change and was secure from calamity.
rows.anchor: their orchard had braved various phases of weather change and had become safe and secure from all calamities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although exegetes unanimously take the phrase to mean they omitted ‘if God wills,’ Islahi rejects that reading: the construction is unsuitable, and istithnāʾ is not explicit enough without contextual evidence.
rows.anchor: Although all the exegetes are unanimous in this interpretation, I personally am not convinced of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads istithnāʾ literally: they swore to take all the fruit and leave none for the poor, rejecting a customary charitable gleaning practice also stated in Leviticus.
rows.anchor: what they swore was that they would pick all the fruit and leave nothing for the poor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath about leaving nothing emphasizes the same stinginess as Quraysh leaders’ forbidding good, especially Abū Lahab and his associates.
rows.anchor: the picture of the stinginess of Abū Lahab and his associates

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing the orchard’s destruction to God signals that the disaster arrived wholly unexpectedly and devastated it in an instant.
rows.anchor: the calamity arrived without the slightest expectation that it would

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The calamity was so devastating that it miraculously reduced the orchard to nothing in a blink; ‘from your Lord’ reassures the Prophet amid Quraysh’s apparent ease.
rows.anchor: it was so devastating in nature that it miraculously routed the orchard to nothingness in the blink of an eye

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable answers those who call the Prophet possessed because they feel secure: punishment can ruin even plans fixed by pledges when people wake to carry them out.
rows.anchor: all of man’s schemes which he devises with the conviction of pledges and oaths are rendered to ruin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for cultivated land can denote the orchard because Arabian orchards included plots sown with crops, so both orchard and field vocabulary fit.
rows.anchor: within orchards, there were pieces of land in which various crops would be sown

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their call challenges the companions to set out immediately if they intend to harvest, warning that delay risks loss.
rows.anchor: if they want to carry out this task, they should not waste time and immediately proceed to the place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The whispered prohibition against a needy person entering repeats the parable’s portrayal of the owners’ stinginess already signaled in verse 18.
rows.anchor: This is another portrayal of their stinginess.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word denotes ardor, freshness, resolve, and a hurried gait; their resolve protects them from the poor, while ‘able’ conveys confidence that ripe fruit and their plan face no obstacle.
rows.anchor: they were fully prepared to protect themselves from being followed by the poor and needy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard was so devastated that they could not recognize it at first and thought they had lost their way; they soon saw that their prized possession was gone.
rows.anchor: All their desires and wishes were dashed to the ground

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘most balanced’ person is the group’s most upright and fair member; even corrupt societies may have a noble soul who repeatedly urges heedfulness and glorification of God.
rows.anchor: Even the most evil of societies has some noble souls who stop people from their ill-ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ comprehensively includes remembering and worshipping God; the others first ignored the counsel, then recognized its truth after seeing the consequences.
rows.anchor: is very comprehensive in nature and encompasses remembering the Almighty as well as worshipping Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their immediate confession acknowledges that success had intoxicated them, making them forget God’s majesty and ignore reminders.
rows.anchor: if someone tried to remind them of it, they never paid heed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their confession parallels Pharaoh’s at the point of drowning; repentance after its proper time is futile.
rows.anchor: This confession is similar to the confession made by the Pharaoh when he and his army were about to drown

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the calamity they blame one another, though all are responsible: some lead disorder and others follow blindly, and all finally admit guilt.
rows.anchor: The only difference is that some lead the way in creating such disorder and others blindly follow them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After blaming one another they hope for a better replacement orchard, but the Qur’an leaves fulfillment unstated; by divine practice, repentance after the deadline is not accepted.
rows.anchor: people who repent after the time for repentance expires are not entertained by the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A similar parable used to address Quraysh appears in al-Kahf 18:32–43.
rows.anchor: a similar parable occurs in verses 32-43 of Sūrah al-Kahf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard’s fate warns Quraysh that the Messenger’s threatened punishment will arrive from an unimaginable direction, like the owners’ calamity, and their later lament will be useless.
rows.anchor: The fact is that it will come to them from where they cannot even imagine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By divine practice, a people’s rejection after a Messenger conclusively conveys truth brings a decisive worldly punishment, followed by a much greater punishment in the Hereafter; Messengers warn of both.
rows.anchor: punishment, which, according to an unalterable divine practice, comes to a people who reject their Messenger after he has conclusively communicated the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing wish expresses sorrow that reckless people deem the inevitable Hereafter unlikely and fail to grasp its terrible punishment.
rows.anchor: these foolish and reckless people regard the Hereafter to be improbable, even though it is inevitable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pious receive gardens of bliss because they feared their Hereafter-accountability and were not seduced by worldly pleasure, unlike the arrogant owners.
rows.anchor: The God-fearing are mentioned in parallel to the arrogant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rewarding the God-fearing follows from divine justice and mercy: equating righteous with wrongdoers, loyal with traitors, or believers with disbelievers would contradict God’s attributes.
rows.anchor: this is but a natural requisite of God’s justice and mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical questions expose the irrational implication that God lacks justice and mercy and does not care whether people are pious; every part of the universe testifies to His providence, mercy, power, and wisdom.
rows.anchor: What a great allegation they make on the Creator, Whose providence, mercy, power and wisdom is borne witness to by every speck

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human intellect and nature reject this verdict; assent means either desires deceive the intellect and override nature, or both intellect and nature have been perverted.
rows.anchor: either they are merely deceiving their intellect while being helpless before their desires and negate their nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh claimed that the Hereafter did not exist, yet if it did they would receive more than in worldly life, treating their leadership as proof of divine favoritism.
rows.anchor: they claimed that in the first place there was no such thing as the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their desires have no rational basis; if scripture guarantees them whatever they want, they should produce it.
rows.anchor: these desires which they nurture in their hearts have no basis in sense and reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With no binding divine oath through Judgment Day, they have no basis for claiming immunity from worldly harm or Hereafter-accountability.
rows.anchor: on what basis do they vainly claim that neither can anyone touch them here in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Promises of Hereafter success are conditional on faith, righteous deeds, and keeping messengers’ covenants; no nation has a guarantee lasting until Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The promises made by the Almighty with nations regarding their success in the Hereafter, are conditional

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s covenant of worldly leadership, affirmed in Torah and Qur’an, excludes wrongdoers among both branches of his descendants, as 2:124 states.
rows.anchor: My covenant does not relate to those among your progeny who wrong their souls by breaking it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s Abrahamic and Ishmaelite descent cannot exempt them from accountability, just as Israelite claims to be God’s children and beloved ones do not, as 5:18 shows.
rows.anchor: would not be held accountable before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge asks Quraysh to name guarantors or associates who would secure their claims, allowing their standing to be assessed; their deities cannot rescue them from God.
rows.anchor: assess their rank and status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an has already discredited the idols Quraysh thought dear to God and able to save them, so they could not name them as guarantors.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh could not have dared to present their names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kashf sāq is a common Arabic idiom for a severe situation; Ḥātim Ṭā’ī’s battle couplet illustrates it with a warrior meeting the crisis head-on.
rows.anchor: a common Arabic idiom to express the severity of a situation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom evokes upheaval forcing modest women to flee with garments raised, exposing shins and jewelry; a cited poem depicts elders forgetting their children and a woman’s shins exposed.
rows.anchor: chaste and decent ladies are forced to flee while raising their legwear, as a result of which, both their shins and the jewelry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day will be cataclysmic for people dreaming of worldly luxuries: those who arrogantly refuse prostration now will then be called to bow but unable.
rows.anchor: whilst these people may be dreaming of having the same luxuries they have here, that Day will be very cataclysmic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day their backs will be too rigid to prostrate even if they wish; downcast eyes and encompassing ignominy will display their helplessness.
rows.anchor: in spite of wanting to prostrate, they will not be able to do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to prostrate humiliates them and shows their denial had no excuse, with their own beings testifying to arrogance and deprivation.
rows.anchor: their own being will bear irrefutable testimony to their arrogance and deprivation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Maʿārij 70:43–44 parallels the scene; its emergence from graves with downcast eyes and ignominy clarifies that ‘the Day the shin is exposed’ means a day of severe upheaval.
rows.anchor: the meaning I have taken

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpreters, relying on a report, take the phrase as God exposing His shin; Islahi rejects that reading in favor of the Arabic idiom for severity.
rows.anchor: interpreted this verse as

rows.speaker: Ibn ‘Abbās
rows.claim: In a report transmitted by ʿIkrimah, Ibn ʿAbbās interprets it as Judgment Day, marked by harshness and brutality.
rows.anchor: A narrative from Ibn ‘Abbās (rta), reported by ‘Ikramah says that it refers to the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: Ibn Jarīr Tabarī
rows.claim: Tabarī records, on Ibn ʿAbbās’s authority, a poet’s opinion supporting the idiomatic reading of sāq.
rows.anchor: the opinion of a poet in support of this opinion

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid also adopts the interpretation that the phrase denotes a severe day.
rows.anchor: has also adopted this meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat is directed to those who rejected the Qur’an, already characterized in 68:15 as calling its recitation ancient tales.
rows.anchor: This is a threat sounded to the rejecters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat also reassures the Prophet: his duty is done, so he can leave the matter to God, whose respite gradually entangles rejecters toward destruction while they mistake it for success.
rows.anchor: the respite which He is now giving them is further entangling them, while they count this to be their success

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s granting respite does not mean the rejecters are beyond His control; His scheme remains sound.
rows.anchor: this does not mean that they are beyond His control; His scheme is very sound

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question expresses amazement that they will not hear the Prophet, who demands no payment; they alone lose the free divine treasure, while he has succeeded before God.
rows.anchor: After all, he is not demanding any payment for this service

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their indifference is challenged: they act as if unseen knowledge guarantees them high status in the Hereafter, but baseless desire and a fool’s paradise lead to doom.
rows.anchor: Do they have the knowledge of the Unseen, that if the Hereafter will come, they will be blessed with high status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same question occurs in al-Ṭūr and is explained there contextually; the context in al-Najm clarifies its meaning completely.
rows.anchor: This verse also occurs in S ūrah al-Ṭūr. I have explained it there in the light of its context
